newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. still facing financial crisis because of U.S.
newsitem.headline: U.N. still facing financial crisis because of U.S.

text.p: Despite anticipated payments from the United States, the United Nations is still facing a financial crisis with a shortfall of at least $2 billion, a senior U.N official said on Wednesday.

"The overall financial situation remains precarious," said Joseph Connor, the U.N. undersecretary for management and administration, adding that the U.N. debt was "still far in excess of prudent financial management."

He said the good news was that the United States was paying at least $100 million more than he had anticipated. But the bad news was that Washington by the end of the year would still owe more than $1.3 billion of the estimated $2.1 billion United Nations debt.
Russia is the world body's second highest debtor, with $300 million, mainly for peacekeeping, having now paid up its regular dues on an instalment plan it instituted.
The U.S. Congress recently approved more than $660 million, of which about $313 million was for 1996 dues, the last instalment of which would not be paid until January.
Also among the new U.S. monies was $282 million for peacekeeping, $50 million for peacekeeping arrears and $20 million for peacekeeping contingencies.

But Connor, the former chief executive officer of the Price Waterhouse accounting firm, said he did not expect most of the U.S. peacekeeping funds until next year because of conditions attached. By that time the United States would owe another batch of peacekeeping contributions for 1997.

The Republican-dominated Congress, to the chagrin of most U.N. members, particularly Europeans and Japan who foot most of the U.N. bill, unilaterally cut Washington's peacekeeping contribution and put conditions on payments.
The omnibus spending bill, signed by President Bill Clinton a week ago, also says the United Nations has to fulfil two out of the following three stipulations:
-- reduce its personnel 10 percent below positions it has in January 1996.
-- make sure the new two-year 1998-99 budget was below $2.6 billion, almost the same as the current one.
-- Save at least $100 million from the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development, regional economic commissions, press information and conference services.
Connor said the United Nations could possibly fulfil the first two demands. But diplomats said it was doubtful whether U.N. members would allow Congress to dictate which programmes should be cut.
"There is a clear danger that the ongoing financial crisis will divert attention from and impact negatively on efforts on internal reform," he said.
To make ends meet, Connor is borrowing from peacekeeping funds which means that about 81 countries who contribute troops are owed about $1.4 billion.
U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said in some cases soldiers from poor nations had been forced to forage for food in fields because their country had no funds.
